claim: Neural oscillations mediate the coordination of activity within and between brain networks, supporting cognition and behaviour.
source: Neural oscillations mediate the coordination of activity within and between brain networks, supporting cognition and behaviour.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural oscillations that draws from established scientific consensus in neuroscience.

claim: Beta oscillations are typically associated with sensorimotor processes.
source: Oscillations in the beta range (13–30 Hz) are typically associated with sensorimotor processes (Barone and Rossiter, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Barone and Rossiter, 2021.

claim: Beta oscillations are prominent over the sensorimotor cortices.
source: they are prominent over the sensorimotor cortices
evidence: This is established knowledge about beta oscillations in neuroscience.

claim: Beta oscillations diminish in amplitude during sensory stimulation or motor execution (termed event-related decrease).
source: diminish in amplitude during sensory stimulation or motor execution (termed event-related decrease)
evidence: This is established knowledge about beta oscillations in neuroscience.

claim: Beta oscillations increase in amplitude (above a baseline level) following stimulus cessation.
source: increase in amplitude (above a baseline level) following stimulus cessation (this is most often termed the post-movement beta rebound [PMBR] [Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999] in relation to movement)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999.

claim: Beta oscillations show abnormalities in autism.
source: studies showing abnormalities across a range of disorders – e.g., autism (Ronconi et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ronconi et al., 2020.

claim: Beta oscillations show abnormalities in multiple sclerosis.
source: multiple sclerosis (Barratt et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Barratt et al., 2017.

claim: Beta oscillations show abnormalities in Parkinson's disease.
source: Parkinson's disease (Little and Brown, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Little and Brown, 2014.

claim: Beta oscillations show abnormalities in Schizophrenia.
source: Schizophrenia (Gascoyne et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gascoyne et al., 2021.

claim: Gaetz et al., 2010, measured beta modulation during index finger movement, showing that the PMBR was diminished in children compared to adults.
source: Gaetz et al., 2010, measured beta modulation during index finger movement, showing that the PMBR was diminished in children compared to adults.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaetz et al., 2010.

claim: Kurz et al., 2016, reported a similar effect when studying 11–19 year olds executing lower limb movement.
source: Kurz et al., 2016, reported a similar effect when studying 11–19 year olds executing lower limb movement.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurz et al., 2016.

claim: Trevarrow et al., 2019, found an age-related increase in the PMBR amplitude in healthy 9–15 year olds.
source: Trevarrow et al., 2019, found an age-related increase in the PMBR amplitude in healthy 9–15 year olds
evidence: Supported by citation to Trevarrow et al., 2019.

claim: Trevarrow et al., 2019, found that the decrease in beta power during movement execution did not modulate with age.
source: further that the decrease in beta power during movement execution did not modulate with age.
evidence: Supported by citation to Trevarrow et al., 2019.

claim: Vakhtin et al., 2015, showed an increase in PMBR amplitude between adolescence and adulthood.
source: Vakhtin et al., 2015, showed an increase in PMBR amplitude between adolescence and adulthood
evidence: Supported by citation to Vakhtin et al., 2015.

claim: Vakhtin et al., 2015, showed that the PMBR trajectory was abnormal in autism.
source: and that this trajectory was abnormal in autism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vakhtin et al., 2015.

claim: Both task-induced beta power loss and the post-stimulus rebound have been consistently observed in adults during tactile stimulation.
source: in the case of tactile stimulation (i.e. sensory stimulation without movement) both task-induced beta power loss and the post-stimulus rebound have been consistently observed in adults (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Gaetz and Cheyne, 2006; Cheyne et al., 2003; van Ede et al., 2010; Salenius et al., 1997; Cheyne, 2013; Kilavik et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Beta amplitude in sensory cortex has been related to attentional processes.
source: Further, beta amplitude in sensory cortex has been related to attentional processes (Bauer et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2006.

claim: Beta amplitude is broadly thought to carry top-down influence on primary areas.
source: and is broadly thought to carry top-down influence on primary areas (Barone and Rossiter, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Barone and Rossiter, 2021.

claim: There is a redistribution of oscillatory power across frequency bands as the brain matures.
source: A separate body of work has assessed neural oscillations in the absence of a task, demonstrating that there is a redistribution of oscillatory power across frequency bands as the brain matures.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent specific claims with citations.

claim: Low-frequency activity tends to decrease with age.

evidence: Supported by citations to Candelaria-Cook et al., 2022; Clarke et al., 2001; Whitford et al., 2007.

claim: High-frequency activity increases with age.
source: Specifically, low-frequency activity tends to decrease, and high-frequency activity increases with age (Candelaria-Cook et al., 2022; Clarke et al., 2001; Whitford et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Candelaria-Cook et al., 2022; Clarke et al., 2001; Whitford et al., 2007.

claim: Increasing beta power with age is most prominent in posterior parietal and occipital regions.
source: These changes are spatially specific, with increasing beta power most prominent in posterior parietal and occipital regions (Hunt et al., 2019; Ott et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2019; Ott et al., 2021.

claim: Beta oscillations are implicated in long-range connectivity.
source: Beta oscillations are also implicated in long-range connectivity (Brookes et al., 2011b; Brookes et al., 2011a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Brookes et al., 2011b; Brookes et al., 2011a.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated increased connectivity strength with age.
source: and previous studies have demonstrated increased connectivity strength with age (Schäfer et al., 2014), particularly in attentional networks (Brookes et al., 2018)

source: MEG detects magnetic fields generated by neural currents, providing assessment of electrical activity with good spatial and millisecond temporal precision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MEG technology.

claim: Traditional MEG sensors operate at low temperature, necessitating the use of fixed 'one-size-fits-all' sensor arrays.
source: However, the sensors traditionally used for field detection operate at low temperature, necessitating the use of fixed 'one-size-fits-all' sensor arrays.
evidence: This is established knowledge about traditional MEG systems.

source: Because the signal declines with the square of distance, smaller head size leads to a reduction in signal (Vorperian et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vorperian et al., 2007 and physical principles.

claim: Movement relative to fixed sensors degrades MEG data quality.
source: In addition, movement relative to fixed sensors degrades data quality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MEG systems.

claim: Scanning young children with traditional MEG systems/SQUIDs is challenging.
source: These limitations mean scanning young children with traditional MEG systems/SQUIDs is challenging

claim: Most MEG studies on neurodevelopment are limited to older children and adolescents.
source: and this has meant that most MEG studies on neurodevelopment are limited to older children and adolescents.
evidence: This is inferred from the challenges of scanning young children with traditional MEG.

claim: EEG measures differences in electrical potential across the scalp.
source: EEG measures differences in electrical potential across the scalp.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EEG technology.

claim: The resistive properties of the skull distort EEG signal topography, limiting spatial resolution.
source: However, the resistive properties of the skull distort signal topography, limiting spatial resolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EEG limitations.

claim: The skull distortion confound in EEG changes with age as the skull increases in thickness.
source: Moreover, this confound changes with age as the skull increases in thickness (Tröndle et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tröndle et al., 2022.

claim: EEG is more susceptible to interference from muscles than MEG, particularly during movement.
source: EEG is also more susceptible to interference from muscles than MEG (Whitham et al., 2007), particularly during movement.

claim: OPMs are small, lightweight and have similar sensitivity to conventional MEG sensors but do not require cryogenics.
source: OPMs are small, lightweight and have similar sensitivity to conventional MEG sensors but do not require cryogenics.

claim: OPM-MEG enables construction of a wearable MEG system.
source: This enables construction of a wearable MEG system (Boto et al., 2018)

source: e.g., Hill et al. showed the viability of OPM-MEG in a 2 year old (Hill et al., 2019)

source: Feys et al. showed advantages for epileptic spike detection in children (Feys et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Feys et al., 2022.

claim: Corvilain et al. demonstrated utility of OPM-MEG even in the first weeks of life.
source: and Corvilain et al. demonstrated utility even in the first weeks of life (Corvilain et al., 2023)

claim: No studies have yet used OPM-MEG in large groups to measure neurodevelopment.
source: However, no studies have yet used OPM-MEG in large groups to measure neurodevelopment.

claim: Recent studies show that the beta rhythm is, in part, driven by discrete punctate events, known as 'bursts'.
source: However, recent studies (Jones, 2016; Sherman et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2017) investigating unaveraged signals show that, rather than a smooth oscillation, the beta rhythm is, in part, driven by discrete punctate events, known as 'bursts'.

claim: Burst probability is altered by a task.
source: Bursts occur with a characteristic probability, which is altered by a task (Little et al., 2019; Seedat et al., 2020)

claim: Bursts are pan-spectral, with components falling across many frequencies.
source: and are not confined to the beta band but are pan-spectral, with components falling across many frequencies (Gascoyne et al., 2021; Seedat et al., 2020)

claim: Functional connectivity is driven by bursts that are coincident in time across spatially separate regions.
source: There is also evidence that functional connectivity is driven by bursts that are coincident in time across spatially separate regions (Seedat et al., 2020)

source: Recent work using EEG has found that, even in children as young as 12 months, beta band activity is driven by bursts (Rayson et al., 2022)

source: Further work, also using EEG, investigated burst activity in infants (9 and 12 months) and adults during observed movement execution, with results showing stimulus-induced decrease in burst rate at all ages, with the largest effects in adults (Rayson et al., 2023)

claim: The OPM-MEG system comprised a maximum of 64 OPMs, each capable of measuring magnetic field independently in three orthogonal orientations, meaning data were recorded using up to 192 channels.
source: Our OPM-MEG system comprised a maximum of 64 OPMs (QuSpin Inc, Colorado, USA), each capable of measuring magnetic field independently in three orthogonal orientations, meaning data were recorded using up to 192 channels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

source: The total weight of the helmet ranged from ~856 g (in the smallest case) to ~906 g (in the largest case).

source: 27 children (aged 2–13 years, 17 female) and 26 adults (aged 21–34 years, 13 female) took part in the study.

source: Following data preprocessing, high-fidelity data were available in 27 children and 24 adults.

source: We removed 19±12% (mean ± standard deviation) of trials in children, and 9±5% of trials in adults due to excessive interference.

source: On average we had 160±10 channels with high-quality data available
